{{Short description|Set of probability distributions}}
In [[theory of probability|probability]] and [[statistics]], the class of '''exponential dispersion models''' ('''EDM'''), also called '''exponential dispersion family''' ('''EDF'''),  is a set of [[probability distribution]]s that represents a generalisation of the [[natural exponential family]].<ref name="J1987">Jørgensen, B. (1987). Exponential dispersion models (with discussion). [[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society]], Series B, 49 (2), 127&ndash;162.</ref><ref>Jørgensen, B. (1992). The theory of exponential dispersion models and analysis of deviance. Monografias de matemática, no. 51.</ref><ref>Marriott, P. (2005) "Local Mixtures and Exponential Dispersion
Models" [https://www.stat.duke.edu/~paul/Paperspdf/dispersion.pdf pdf]</ref>
Exponential dispersion models play an important role in [[statistical theory]], in particular in [[generalized linear model]]s because they have a special structure which enables deductions to be made about appropriate [[statistical inference]].

==Definition==
===Univariate case===
There are two versions to formulate an exponential dispersion model.
====Additive exponential dispersion model====
In the univariate case, a real-valued random variable <math>X</math> belongs to the '''additive exponential dispersion model''' with canonical parameter <math>\theta</math> and index parameter <math>\lambda</math>, <math>X \sim \mathrm{ED}^*(\theta, \lambda)</math>, if its [[probability density function]] can be written as

:<math> f_X(x\mid\theta, \lambda) = h^*(\lambda,x) \exp\left(\theta x - \lambda A(\theta)\right) \,\! .</math>

====Reproductive exponential dispersion model====
The distribution of the transformed random variable <math>Y=\frac{X}{\lambda}</math> is called '''reproductive exponential dispersion model''', <math>Y \sim \mathrm{ED}(\mu, \sigma^2)</math>, and is given by

:<math> f_Y(y\mid\mu, \sigma^2) = h(\sigma^2,y) \exp\left(\frac{\theta y - A(\theta)}{\sigma^2}\right) \,\! ,</math>

with <math>\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{\lambda}</math> and <math>\mu = A'(\theta)</math>, implying <math>\theta = (A')^{-1}(\mu)</math>.
The terminology ''dispersion model'' stems from interpreting <math>\sigma^2</math> as ''dispersion parameter''. For fixed parameter <math>\sigma^2</math>, the <math>\mathrm{ED}(\mu, \sigma^2)</math> is a [[natural exponential family]].

===Multivariate case===
In the multivariate case, the ''n''-dimensional random variable <math>\mathbf{X}</math> has a probability density function of the following form<ref name=J1987/>

:<math> f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta}, \lambda) = h(\lambda,\mathbf{x}) \exp\left(\lambda(\boldsymbol\theta^\top \mathbf{x} - A(\boldsymbol\theta))\right) \,\!,</math>

where the parameter <math>\boldsymbol\theta</math> has the same dimension as <math>\mathbf{X}</math>.

==Properties==
===Cumulant-generating function===
The [[cumulant-generating function]] of <math>Y\sim\mathrm{ED}(\mu,\sigma^2)</math> is given by

:<math>K(t;\mu,\sigma^2) = \log\operatorname{E}[e^{tY}] = \frac{A(\theta+\sigma^2 t)-A(\theta)}{\sigma^2}\,\! ,</math>

with <math>\theta = (A')^{-1}(\mu)</math>

===Mean and variance===
Mean and variance of <math>Y\sim\mathrm{ED}(\mu,\sigma^2)</math> are given by

:<math> \operatorname{E}[Y]= \mu = A'(\theta) \,, \quad \operatorname{Var}[Y] = \sigma^2 A''(\theta) = \sigma^2 V(\mu)\,\! ,</math>

with unit variance function <math>V(\mu) = A''((A')^{-1}(\mu))</math>.

===Reproductive===
If <math>Y_1,\ldots, Y_n</math> are [[i.i.d.]] with <math>Y_i\sim\mathrm{ED}\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{w_i}\right)</math>, i.e. same mean <math>\mu</math> and different weights <math>w_i</math>, the weighted mean is again an <math>\mathrm{ED}</math> with

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{w_i Y_i}{w_{\bullet}} \sim \mathrm{ED}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{w_\bullet}\right) \,\! ,</math>

with <math>w_\bullet = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i</math>. Therefore <math>Y_i</math> are called ''reproductive''.

===Unit deviance===
The [[probability density function]] of an <math>\mathrm{ED}(\mu, \sigma^2)</math> can also be expressed in terms of the '''unit [[Deviance (statistics)|deviance]]''' <math>d(y,\mu)</math> as

:<math> f_Y(y\mid\mu, \sigma^2) = \tilde{h}(\sigma^2,y) \exp\left(-\frac{d(y,\mu)}{2\sigma^2}\right) \,\! ,</math>

where the unit deviance takes the special form <math>d(y,\mu) = y f(\mu) + g(\mu) + h(y)</math> or in terms of the unit variance function as <math>d(y,\mu) = 2 \int_\mu^y\! \frac{y-t}{V(t)} \,dt</math>.

==Examples==
Many very common probability distributions belong to the class of EDMs, among them are: [[normal distribution]], [[binomial distribution]], [[Poisson distribution]], [[negative binomial distribution]], [[gamma distribution]], [[inverse Gaussian distribution]], and [[Tweedie distribution]].
